p: Editions differ on the order of the two names. The meaning does not change.

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT (editions only)
Textus Receptus (KJV), Byzantine majority text (editions only)

why: Paul uses both orders in his letters. The Plain English Translation follows the SBLGNT and NA28.

a: If we are in trouble, it is for your comfort and salvation. If we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which does its work in you as you patiently endure the very sufferings we also suffer.
t: Where does "which does its work in you" belong?
p: The editions arrange the clauses of this verse in two orders, and the KJV follows the other one.

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Westcott-Hort (editions only)
readings.orig: εἴτε δὲ θλιβόμεθα, ὑπὲρ τῆς ὑμῶν παρακλήσεως καὶ σωτηρίας· εἴτε παρακαλούμεθα, ὑπὲρ τῆς ὑμῶν παρακλήσεως τῆς ἐνεργουμένης ἐν ὑπομονῇ …
readings.en: If we are in trouble, it is for your comfort and salvation. If we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which does its work in you as you patiently endure
readings.plain: If we are in trouble, it is for your comfort and salvation. If we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which does its work in you as you patiently endure the very sufferings we also suffer.

readings.w: Textus Receptus (KJV), Byzantine majority text; the Tyndale House GNT and Tregelles also depart from the SBLGNT order (editions only)
readings.orig: εἴτε δὲ θλιβόμεθα, ὑπὲρ τῆς ὑμῶν παρακλήσεως καὶ σωτηρίας τῆς ἐνεργουμένης ἐν ὑπομονῇ … εἴτε παρακαλούμεθα, ὑπὲρ τῆς ὑμῶν παρακλήσεως καὶ σωτηρίας
readings.en: If we are in trouble, it is for your comfort and salvation, which does its work in you as you patiently endure the same sufferings we suffer. If we are comforted, it is for your comfort and salvation.
readings.plain: If we are in trouble, it is for your comfort and salvation, which does its work in you as you patiently endure the very sufferings we also suffer. If we are comforted, it is for your comfort and salvation.

why: Both orders give the same general sense: Paul's troubles and his comfort both serve the Corinthians. The Plain English Translation follows the SBLGNT and NA28, in which the "work in endurance" belongs to the comfort.

p: The KJV reads "doth deliver," a present tense. Most editions read the future.

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles (editions only)
Textus Receptus (KJV), Byzantine majority text (editions only)

why: The next clause has the future too ("he will rescue us again"), which fits the first reading. The Plain English Translation follows the SBLGNT and NA28.

p: The Byzantine text has "your" where the other editions have "our." The KJV agrees with the SBLGNT.

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, Textus Receptus (KJV) (editions only)

why: The sense is close: the thanks rise for the gift given to Paul and his team, or for the gift given to the Corinthians. The Plain English Translation follows the SBLGNT.

p: Editions differ on one word: holiness (SBLGNT) or simplicity, openness (NA28, KJV, per this project's edition marks).

readings.w: SBLGNT, THGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles (editions only)
NA28, Textus Receptus (KJV), Byzantine majority text (editions only)

why: The Plain English Translation follows the SBLGNT and so departs from the word-for-word line, which reads "openness" (haplotes). "Simplicity" may have come in from the same word in 8:2, 9:11 and 11:3, where Paul does use it, and the two Greek words (hagiotes, haplotes) look alike when written. Both fit the context, and "single-hearted openness" is the sense of the other reading. The site's word list shows only which editions print each reading; it names no manuscripts.

p: Some editions leave out "our." The KJV reads "the day of the Lord Jesus."

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Westcott-Hort (editions only)
Textus Receptus (KJV), Byzantine majority text, Tyndale House GNT, Tregelles (editions only)

why: The meaning is the same. The Plain English Translation follows the SBLGNT.

Westcott-Hort (editions only)

why: The two words differ by a few letters. "Grace" can mean a favor or benefit, which fits a second visit as a second gift to the church. The Plain English Translation follows the SBLGNT and NA28.
b: The Textus Receptus and the Byzantine text also read "have" (echete) where the others read "get" (schete); the English difference is small.

a: That is why the "Amen" also goes up to God through him
t: "Therefore also through him" or "and in him"?
p: The KJV reads "and in him Amen." The oldest text has a stronger link: "therefore."

readings.w: Textus Receptus (KJV), Byzantine majority text (editions only)
readings.plain: And in him is the "Amen" to God

why: The shorter, sharper text with "therefore" and "through" explains why Christians say Amen through Christ (as in prayers that end "through Jesus Christ"). The other reading may come from copying the "in him" of the line before. The Plain English Translation follows the SBLGNT and NA28.

p: The Byzantine text reads "the rest" where the other editions, and the Textus Receptus behind the KJV, read "the many."

Byzantine majority text (editions only)

a: tablets that are hearts of flesh
p: The Textus Receptus (and so the KJV) has "of the heart" in the singular; the other editions have the plural "hearts" in apposition to "tablets."

readings.w: NA28, NA27, SBLGNT, THGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, Byzantine majority text (editions only)
readings.plain: tablets that are hearts of flesh

p: The editions differ on the grammar of "glory" in the first half of 3:9. The KJV follows the Byzantine form.

readings.w: NA28, NA27, SBLGNT, THGNT, Tregelles (editions only)
readings.orig: εἰ γὰρ τῇ διακονίᾳ τῆς κατακρίσεως δόξα
readings.en: for if to the ministry of condemnation [there was] glory

readings.w: Textus Receptus (KJV), Byzantine majority text (which also add "in" before "glory" in the second half) (editions only)
readings.orig: εἰ γὰρ ἡ διακονία τῆς κατακρίσεως δόξα
readings.en: for if the ministry of condemnation [is] glory

why: The dative ("to the ministry... glory") is the harder reading and gives "had glory"; the nominative makes the ministry itself the glory. The point of the "how much more" argument is the same. The Plain English Translation follows the SBLGNT.
b: The project's edition marks show that Westcott-Hort also does not read the dative.

a: because in Christ it is being set aside
p: One small difference decides what is being set aside. The critical editions read "because"; the Textus Receptus and Byzantine text read "which," and the KJV follows them.

readings.w: NA28, NA27, SBLGNT, THGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles (editions only)
readings.en: because in Christ it is being set aside
readings.plain: because in Christ it is being set aside

readings.w: Textus Receptus (KJV), Byzantine majority text (editions only)
readings.en: which in Christ is being set aside
readings.plain: which is set aside in Christ

why: With "because," the reason the veil is not lifted is that what is being set aside is set aside only in Christ; the subject of "is being set aside" is then not named, and it can be the veil, the old covenant, or the old order. With "which," the veil itself is what Christ removes, as 3:16 says. The Plain English Translation follows the critical editions and keeps "it" open; see the note at 3:7.

a: who said, "Out of darkness light will shine,"
t: "light will shine" or "commanded light to shine"?
p: The KJV has God commanding light to shine out of darkness. The older text has a future verb inside the quotation.

why: The future tense belongs to a quotation, and the infinitive in the other reading may be a scribe's smoothing of it into a report of Genesis 1:3. The Plain English Translation follows the SBLGNT.

p: The KJV reads "the face of Jesus Christ." The editions are split.

NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Textus Receptus (KJV), Byzantine majority text (editions only)

t: "the dying of Jesus" or "of the Lord Jesus"?
p: The KJV reads "the dying of the Lord Jesus."

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles (editions only)
Textus Receptus (KJV), Byzantine majority text (editions only)
readings.en: the dying of the Lord Jesus
readings.plain: the dying of the Lord Jesus

why: "Lord" looks like a common addition. The second half of the verse says only "the life of Jesus," which supports the shorter text. The Plain English Translation follows the SBLGNT.

p: The KJV reads "raise up us also by Jesus." The better-attested text says "with."

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles (editions only)
Textus Receptus (KJV), Byzantine majority text (editions only)

why: "With Jesus" is the harder reading, since Paul has just said that God "raised" Jesus, and it matches Paul's idea of sharing Christ's resurrection (Romans 6:4-5, 8). "Through Jesus" is the easier text. The Plain English Translation follows the SBLGNT.

p: One letter changes the sense: "if we are clothed" or "if we have taken it off." The editions are split.

readings.w: SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, Textus Receptus (KJV), Byzantine majority text (editions only)
readings.en: if indeed also having put on

readings.w: NA27 and NA28 (editions only)
readings.en: if indeed also having taken off
readings.plain: If indeed we have taken it off

why: The editions are divided. NA27 and NA28 print "having taken off"; the SBLGNT, Tyndale House and the Textus Receptus (the KJV) have "having put on." The Plain English Translation follows the SBLGNT, and so departs from the word-for-word line, which was built on the NA text and reads "having put off." Two arguments can be made. For "taken off": it is the harder reading, since it makes the sentence say very little ("if we have taken it off, we will not be found naked"), and a scribe may have smoothed it into "put on." For "put on": "taken off" may itself be an early change made to avoid the near-tautology "if we are clothed, we will not be found naked," and "put on" fits "dressed over" in 5:4. No scholar is cited for either argument, and the site's word list names no manuscripts. On either reading Paul's fear is of being unclothed.
b: Many commentators note that the two readings differ by a single pair of letters (en- or ek-) and that the scribes could easily have confused them.

p: The Textus Receptus and Byzantine text have a different word for the second term.

Textus Receptus (KJV), Byzantine majority text (editions only)

a: one died for all, and so all died
t: "one died for all" or "if one died for all"?
p: The KJV reads "if one died for all, then were all dead," a conditional. The critical editions state it as a fact.

readings.w: NA28, NA27, SBLGNT, THGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles (editions only)
readings.orig: ὅτι εἷς ὑπὲρ πάντων ἀπέθανεν· ἄρα οἱ πάντες ἀπέθανον

readings.w: Textus Receptus (KJV), Byzantine majority text (editions only)
readings.orig: ὅτι εἰ εἷς ὑπὲρ πάντων ἀπέθανεν, ἄρα οἱ πάντες ἀπέθανον
readings.en: that if one died for all, then all died
readings.plain: if one died for all, then all died

why: The "if" reading is the KJV's. In Paul the death of the one for all is not in doubt (compare 1 Corinthians 15:3), so "if" would mean "since." The Plain English Translation follows the SBLGNT. The reading matters for the card on this verse, which asks for whom Christ died.

a: new things have come into being
t: "new things have come" or "all things have become new"?
p: The KJV reads "behold, all things are become new." The older text has no "all things."

p: The KJV reads "by Jesus Christ."
